implementation_notes: The full structure is hand-written: one bounded ring buffer guarded by a pthread_mutex_t with two condition variables (not-empty and not-full), plus N worker threads that wait for a message, dequeue under the lock, then process it outside the lock. The mutex is what replaces the broker: only one worker can complete a dequeue, so exactly one consumer gets each message, and the not-full condition gives producers backpressure.
pitfalls: Wait predicates must be re-checked in a while loop: spurious wakeups and missed signals otherwise hand a worker an empty queue or park it forever.
Holding the mutex while processing serialises the pool; dequeue under the lock, work outside it.
A job is removed before it is handled, so a crash mid-handler loses it - C has no redelivery unless the queue is durable or failed jobs are explicitly re-enqueued.

variants.name: POSIX message queue (kernel hand-off)
variants.implementation_notes: POSIX realtime message queues move the delivery rule into the kernel: when several threads or processes are blocked in mq_receive on one queue, exactly one of them receives each message, so the competing-consumer contract needs no hand-written locking. Link with -lrt and respect the queue's own limits (mq_maxmsg, mq_msgsize, /dev/mqueue accounting); the queue is not durable across reboot, so at-least-once semantics still require an acknowledgement protocol or a broker.
pitfalls: POSIX queues are not durable across reboot and have small default capacities; they buffer work but do not guarantee it.
mq_receive copies into a caller buffer sized for the queue's mq_msgsize - a short buffer fails with EMSGSIZE rather than truncating.
The kernel discards a message as soon as one receiver has read it, so a receiver crashing mid-handle still loses the message.
